title: Thiebou Jenn
localName: Ceebu jën — thiéboudienne, riz au poisson
author: Pierre Thiam
desc: Senegal's national dish and, in its author's words, the one dish that unites all Senegalese — the rice finishes in the fish broth and the crust from the pot bottom is served in its own bowl.
longDesc: A whole five-pound thioff or grouper is cut into seven steaks, each slit twice and stuffed with rof — a pounded paste of parsley, garlic, onion and scallion. The stew base is onions, green pepper and two cups of tomato paste cooked down on low until the oil separates and rises to the surface and the paste has turned a dark orange. Fish, hibiscus and scotch bonnets poach in it; then guedj and yeet, the fermented fish and shellfish, go in for ten minutes. The vegetables follow, then two cups of broken rice are steamed over the broth in a cheesecloth-lined colander before being stirred into it to finish. Serves ten.
ingredients: 1 large whole thioff or grouper, about 5 lb, scaled and gutted, cut into 7 steaks about 1 1/2 in thick, head and tail reserved
1 green bell pepper, seeded and chopped
2 palm-sized pieces guedj — dried, salted, smoked fish (SEN088)
2 pieces yeet, rinsed — dried, fermented shellfish (SEN089)
// or substitute 1/4 to 1/2 cup Vietnamese or Thai fish sauce, to taste
1/2 head green cabbage, cut into 3 wedges
1 turnip, peeled and cut into thick wedges
1 small butternut squash, peeled, seeded and cut into large chunks
1 yuca, 4 to 5 in, peeled and cut into large chunks
2 carrots, peeled and cut into large chunks
1 handful shelled tamarind pods, or 1 tbsp tamarind paste
2 cups broken white rice, or jasmine or basmati, washed and drained
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a blender
Large serving platter and a separate bowl
steps: Blend or pound the rof coarse.
Cut two 2-inch slits in each fish steak and fill each with about 1 teaspoon of rof. Coat the fish, including the head and tail, and refrigerate.
Heat the oil over medium-high. Add two pinches of salt, the onions, the green pepper and the tomato paste.

Lower the heat to low and cook 10 to 15 minutes, stirring often and adding 1 to 2 tablespoons of water if needed — until the oil separates and rises to the surface and the tomato paste has turned a dark orange.
Add the 5 cups of water, bring to the boil, reduce, and simmer about 30 minutes.
Add the fish, head and tail, the hibiscus, the scotch bonnets and a pinch of black pepper. Cook uncovered over medium about 15 minutes, until the fish is cooked through.
Remove the fish to a bowl, cover and keep warm.
Add the guedj and yeet, or the fish sauce. Partially cover and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the cabbage, turnip, eggplant, squash, yuca, carrots and bitter eggplants. Return to the boil, season, reduce and simmer 20 minutes, until tender.
Add the okra and cook 10 minutes more.
Move the vegetables to the fish bowl with a few ladles of broth and the tamarind.
Set a cheesecloth-lined colander of rice over the simmering broth, cover, and steam 10 to 15 minutes.

Stir the rice into the broth, bring to the boil, lower to low, skim the excess oil and adjust the broth so it just covers the rice. Cover tightly and cook about 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Mound the rice on a platter with the fish and vegetables in the centre and lime wedges around.
Scrape the crust from the bottom of the pot and serve it in a separate bowl.
chefTips: The tomato paste stage is the dish. Two cups of paste cooked on low until the oil separates and rises and the colour turns dark orange is what makes this red rather than merely tomatoey — rush it and you get a raw, sharp broth.
Steam the rice over the broth before stirring it in. That two-stage treatment is why the grains stay separate in a dish with this much liquid.
Adjust the broth so it JUST covers the rice before the final twenty minutes. More than that and it goes to porridge.
The crust from the pot bottom — the khoukhou — is served in its own bowl and is the prized part. Scrape it; do not soak the pot.

Guedj and yeet are the fermented backbone. If you cannot get them, the author's own substitution is a quarter to half a cup of Vietnamese or Thai fish sauce, which is a fair swap for the fermented note.
Broken rice, not whole grain, is traditional and it matters: the broken grains absorb the broth faster and bind the dish.
The author notes this version is more traditional than the one in his earlier book, so where his two printings disagree, this is the one he stands behind.
commonMistakes: Under-cooking the tomato paste, so the oil never separates.
Adding raw rice straight to the broth without the steaming stage.
Too much broth at the final covered cook.
Leaving the fish in while the vegetables cook, which shreds it.
Washing the crust off the pot bottom.
sources: Adapted from 'Thiebou Jenn', published in two places from the same book: southernfoodways.org (SFA page carries NO author byline; the excerpt is credited to Pierre Thiam and Jennifer Sit, 'Senegal: Modern Senegalese Recipes from the Source to the Bowl', Lake Isle Press, 2015; metadata date 17 September 2015, no visible date on the page), and explorepartsunknown.com, 'Recipe: Thiebou Jenn', BYLINE AS PRINTED 'Pierre Thiam', photographer Evan Sung, 4 April 2017. Yield as printed on both: 'Serves 10'. Rof: 'makes about 1 cup' on both.

SOURCING STATUS: this is the only ceebu jen in this collection with genuine TWO-SOURCE corroboration. Strict verbatim transcription was REFUSED on both domains by the retrieval layer's ~125-character quote cap, but the two INDEPENDENT publications carry the identical recipe and agree on every comparable quantity — 5 lb fish, 1/4 to 1/2 cup fish sauce, serves 10, and the times 10-15 / 30 / 15 / 10 / 20 / 10 / 10-15 / 20 minutes. Those shared figures are therefore treated as TWO-PASS by cross-publication agreement rather than by transcription.

THE DONENESS CUES, quoted as short fragments because longer quotation was refused: 'until oil separates and rises to the surface'; the tomato paste 'has turned a dark orange'; 'until the fish is cooked through'; 'until tender' for the vegetables; 'until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.' NO oven or internal temperatures appear anywhere — heat levels only, low, medium and medium-high.

THE AUTHORS' OWN FRAMING, quoted: they call thiebou jenn Senegal's national dish and 'the one dish that unites all Senegalese', served daily in many households, each with its own version. Thioff is named as the traditional fish. The authors state plainly that this version is MORE TRADITIONAL than the one in Thiam's earlier cookbook 'Yolele!', which is why it is the one published here.
A DOCUMENTED RESTAURANT VARIANT, recorded: the Explore Parts Unknown printing adds a note on a whole fried-fish version served at Chez Loutcha in Dakar.

THE UNESCO RECORD, which is a cultural source and NOT a recipe: 'Ceebu Jën, a culinary art of Senegal', UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, BYLINE: UNESCO ICH (organisation), 'Inscribed in 2021 (16.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity'. It names fish steak, broken rice, dried fish, mollusc, onions, parsley, garlic, chilli pepper, tomatoes, carrots, eggplant, cassava, sweet potato, okra and bay leaf, with NO quantities and NO method. Its origin claim, quoted: 'Ceebu jën is a dish that originated in the fishing communities on the Island of Saint-Louis in Senegal.' It also records that 'recipes vary from one region to the next'; that 'The quality of the fish and the choice of vegetables are determined by the importance of the event'; that 'The recipe and techniques are traditionally passed down from mother to daughter'; and that 'The ceebu jën dish and associated practices are viewed as an affirmation of Senegalese identity.' On table manners it records that eating by hand is common in most families while restaurants use spoons or forks, that sitting with a raised knee is forbidden, that the bowl is held in the left hand, and that rice grains must not be dropped. NOTE that UNESCO does NOT name the red/white variants at all, confirmed across two passes.

ON PENDA MBAYE, an attribution this collection records as contested in both its printings rather than as fact. READING A, the UNESCO nomination file ICH-02 (Senegal, September 2020), TWO-PASS: 'Tout le monde attribue l'invention de ce mets à Penda Mbaye, une cuisinière du village de Guet-Ndar' — everyone attributes the invention of this dish to Penda Mbaye, a cook of the village of Guet-Ndar. READING B, Kitchen Butterfly, 19 November 2014, whose page byline is 'Kitchen Butterfly' and which attributes this material within itself to Kiratiana Freelon writing on Bonjour Paris, SINGLE-PASS: 'According to oral tradition, Thiéboudienne is the creation of one woman from Saint Louis, Senegal'; 'Penda Mbaye, a cook at the colonial governor's residence, created the dish of fish and vegetables first using barley.' THE DISAGREEMENT: reading A makes her a cook of a fishing village, reading B a cook at the colonial governor's residence, and reading B adds that the FIRST GRAIN WAS BARLEY rather than rice. Reading A's own account of the grain differs again, describing rice imported from Indochina displacing local food crops. Both are recorded; neither is chosen. Both printings are themselves hedged — 'Tout le monde attribue' in one, 'oral tradition' in the other.

ON THE JOLLOF ORIGIN QUESTION, and this entry is where it belongs because every other jollof in this collection points back here. The claim that ceebu jen is the ancestor of jollof rice is widely repeated and thinly evidenced. What the sources actually show: Kitchen Butterfly gives the fullest treatment and is EXPLICITLY HYPOTHETICAL about it; Yummy Medley states the claim flatly with no citation; English Wikipedia carries the claim resting on a single citation; a Gambiana account offers a competing Gambian/Wolof version that REJECTS the Senegalese framing; and a Quartz headline makes a claim its own body text does not support. Note that this collection's Ghanaian party-jollof entry quotes its author saying it is 'always amusing to read that this is the "national dish" of any specific West African country, since it belongs to the whole region', and that the earliest PRINTED jollof recipe traced in this collection is in a 1910 colonial cookery manual. The honest position recorded here: Senegalese origin is a widely held claim, not a documented fact, and the dish belongs to the region.
A LEAD NOT CHASED: a Substack post, '1949books.substack.com/p/penda-mbaye-legende-culinaire-et', surfaced in search and was not fetched.
storage: 3 days refrigerated, components separate. The rice dries out faster than the stew.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the fish and vegetables gently in a little broth.
healthBenefits: Grouper is high in protein, selenium and vitamin B12 and low in saturated fat.
Eight or nine vegetables in one pot, which is unusual for any single dish.
Cooked tomato paste at this concentration is very high in lycopene.
culturalNote: Ceebu jen was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2021, and the nomination file traces it to the fishing communities of Saint-Louis island. It is eaten from a shared bowl, by hand, with the left hand holding the bowl and the right doing the work — and there are rules: no raised knee, no dropped grains. Its author calls it the one dish that unites all Senegalese, which is a large claim he is entitled to make.
